title: A Blueprint for Weird Teachers, Schools, and Districts
author: Science of Reading Classroom
source: Science of Reading Classroom Substack, January 26, 2026
summary: Effective teachers share one core attribute: intense curiosity that drives them to continuously tinker with instruction, content, and delivery, constantly learn new approaches despite current success, and seek connections with like-minded peers to understand what successful teachers do. School and district leaders can cultivate teacher curiosity by allocating regular, dedicated paid contract time for discussing instructional practice, maintaining relentless focus on pedagogy rather than ancillary concerns, structuring these conversations around shared texts (video, lesson plans, student work), building explicit culture of experimentation, and identifying high-performing teachers (those exiting most students from intervention or achieving 80+ percent benchmark rates) and giving them agency to teach other teachers. This approach turns isolated pockets of excellence into systemic improvement.
points: The smartest and most effective teachers share intense curiosity despite working in systems that don't intentionally reward it; they constantly tinker with instruction, seek professional learning even after success, and look for ways to scale their work beyond their own classroom.

School leaders should allocate regular, dedicated paid contract time specifically for teachers to discuss, share, and explore instructional practice; without dedicated time, teachers cannot develop and sustain curiosity about pedagogy.

Professional development structures should center on relentless focus on instructional practice using shared texts (video, lesson plans, student work) and require teachers to make plans to try new routines in their own contexts, then return to debrief application and refine.

Leaders should explicitly encourage and build culture of experimentation and tinkering; many high-performing teachers are using instructional approaches that bump against existing rules, and finding these teachers who are already experimenting is the entry point for systemic change.

School leaders should identify high-performing teachers by examining student outcome data (exit rates from intervention, benchmark achievement, consistent outperformance), give these 'weird teachers' agency and visibility, and position them to teach other teachers; that is how culture of excellence and curiosity begins.
quotes: When people ask me what I do, I tell them I run a fellowship program and a professional development program that lets me work with some of the smartest and most effective reading teachers in the country. There's the reading specialist who exited nearly 30 students from intervention last year.
Results like these aren't normal. My teachers are, for lack of a better word, weird. (I'm fond of telling them this.) And they're weird in a way that every school and district should want.

When I think about what these teachers have in common, I can identify one core shared attribute: they're intensely curious, despite working in a system that doesn't intentionally reward or cultivate curiosity. In practice, this means these teachers are always tinkering with their instruction, their content, and their delivery.

Teachers need regular and dedicated contract (i.e. paid) time to discuss, share, and explore their instructional practice. These conversations and explorations won't just happen organically, at least at first. In order to be curious about something, you need time to think about it.

Find the teachers who are using the secret curriculum, and start there. And once you've found them, give them agency and put them in a position to teach other teachers. That's how this work begins.” Archived from Science of Reading Classroom Substack on April 21, 2026 by Tim.
